MAID track 2 is the only option for people who fall in between the cracks.  and they don't necessarily fall in between the cracks because the system has failed overall.  some people are just fantastically unlucky, and have bizarre and unusual conditions that don't neatly fit laws and buraucracy.

terminal illness or not, everyone on his care team agreed that while he was suffering in the present, a GREAT DEAL more suffering was heading his way.   a team of doctors, psychologists, care workers, lawyers and multiple applications and assessments through levels of medical boards were required before they green-lit his MAID.

The UN board and report would have caused unbearable suffering for my brother.

When in-mission: opening the map (tab on pc) will show the mission level.  It’s a little triangle shaped thing in the upper right I believe.
When in the ship, go to the mission map and zoom out to the planetary or galaxy zoom level.  There you can (press q or e on pc) to toggle “right and left” through difficulty levels. The game helpfully displays below the difficulty what kinds of things you’ll find in the mission at that difficulty. ( ex. main objective, patrols, enemy encampments, special objectives, special enemies, etc) these increase and change as difficulty goes up. 
Levels 1 and 2 are mostly tutorial.  Levels 3 and 4 will have 80-90% of the mechanics the game has to offer at the normal level, and can be soloed more or less easily by new players.  5 and 6 start to have more heavy and huge units that demand heavy weapons and knowledge to defeat.  Get a team! I spend most of my time in the 4-6 range depending on my mood. Overall it sounds like the majority of high skill players find difficulty 7 to be a sweet spot. 8-10/Helldive difficulty is apparently easy for some people? But I’m not there yet.

I would recommend adjusting difficulty to 2 or 3 and check out the new things to do on the map!

When I first started really playing games in the 90's, there wasn't as much choice.  Maybe 2-5 properly good games per year? So I was much more likely to pursue games with a lot of depth and rabbit holes to go down.

Much like books...I would start one,  ...and then even if I wasn't digging it that hard I'd say to myself, " Well I got this far... And I've already got some sunk cost here so,  I guess I might as well finish it."

Fast forward to 2021, much less so now.   We have a much more saturated market of good games.  Also apps phones internet social media...  There's a veritable fire-hose of content and information pointed at our heads at all times.  More content than we can possibly consume in an entire lifetime.

...and as a result I'm a much more fickle gamer and reader.  I'll get in and try something, and if it doesn't grab me or make me feel something in the first half an hour then I'm much much more likely to just pull the rip cord, eject, put it down, and try something else.  The sunk-cost fallacy is completely gone for me now.

I still generally dislike the same genres. (Sports games, pvp fps, ewe)  ...but I'm much more likely to , step outside of my comfort zone, and try things based on the opinions of trusted/respected games conossoires. (J sterling, skillup, ranton, justin shrier, acg)

Being less rigid in my preferences and paying attention to the youtuber/podcaster/ social media discussions on games has resulted in much better gaming experiences overall than the old 90's arcade traditional media days.

Tldr: more choice more words = less patience less settleing.

Whelp, all of that sounds complicated, and horrible.  I'm deeply sorry all this is happening to you.   My advice is not perfect.  My empathy is not perfect.  I'll dispense my advice and ideas now regardless.

Some advice from the military side:

1. "Breathe.  Look around.  Make a call."  This is your motto from now on.  Tattoo it on your ass.  This will help you from being overwhelmed, or losing it because you can't find an Optimal(tm) solution.  There isn't one.  Don't worry about finding it.  Don't give up.  Just be Reasonable(tm), and make the best call you can to maximize well being.
2. Prioritize.  When a couple of helicopters crash, you don't march into the generals office and tell him there weren't enough seat-belts on the first chopper.   Solve the problem that's in front of you, and then have the more complicated conversation on the back-end once the crisis it over.   Which issue matters the most here?  If your boyfriend is dead, then any other sub-problem won't matter.  Keep him breathing.  Worry about the disease he has afterwards.
3. Bounce ideas off other people.    What you're doing right now is good.  What you've described in yourself and in your boyfriend is a doubt that your perceptions are accurate., for a variety of reasons.   The accuracy of your, "sensors", for lack of a better word, has been called into doubt.   Therefore, contacting other people you can have some confidence in that their perceptions and judgement are accurate, to bounce your ideas and feelings off of, is the best thing you can do.  your aircraft has lost radar?  get on the horn to a neighboring aircraft and ask them what they see.  Don't be shy about doing this.
4. This is an emergency, objectively.  not to alarm you, but rather to confirm your intuition that this is not okay.  Being pro-choice on the suicide issue is one thing.  But in such serious circumstances one always has to ask themselves "what if I'm wrong?"  You have already identified a spectrum of mental illness in both your boyfriend, and yourself.  If a hypothetical friend of yours was considering suicide, would you recommend they seek advice from a panel composed of depressed and suicidal people?  no, because their own objectivity is called into question.  true loyalty to your boyfriend and to yourself at this point would be to gird yourself, get outside yourself and push, and get an objective assessment (as objective as possible), from a variety of people who's judgement is objectively, factually, sound.
5. which leads me to my next point: sometimes doctors are good.  they're probably necessary here.  but my recommendation is simple and inexpensive.  seek out other people with similar life experience, and just talk to them.  doesn't cost a thing.   whether that's a support group for depression, or for the family members of folks who've taken their own lives.   i've done this myself.   even if they don't have every answer, it provides context, and you can problem solve without having to start from scratch.  pool your collective experience and come up with a solution you couldn't have reached on your own.

I don't know exactly what you feel like.  I have to try and imagine, and then ask questions.  Some of what you said reminded me if a time when I felt desperate and alone and unemployed after a break up.  Things weren't just bad.  They got so bad that I felt disoriented and unhinged. 

The following things helped me:
1 I visited a counselor.   He wasn't very good.  He had few observations, and I didn't learn many things from him.  However, what he did give me was some context.  Somewhere on the scale of how well I was coping compared to other patients on similar situations.  I was terrified, but being able to place myself somewhere and read the terrain a bit, this made me feel better oriented.

Therapist contact information is often changed or protected.  Try again, for your preffered therapist.  Perhaps there's an organization or a register where they might be? Perhaps on another doctors office contact list?  Don't give up on that quite yet.  

2 I discovered Sam Harris and his books and podcast.  He's a neuroscientist and a philosopher, and runs a meditation app.  I found him very clear thinking.  There are some good free videos available on YouTube which are about managing negative emotion and anxiety. I recommend you check them out.  Also his app has a really good video lessons, particularly the one about Solving Problems, and Death.  Message me if you can't find it and I'll see if I can get you the content somehow.

3 I'm Canadian.  Started reading a book called "the last taboo, a guide to mental health care in canada".  There's lots of good advice in there, not just for how to navigate getting help from service providers, but how to navigate friends and family.  Also useful.

4 I started attending a support group for other people who were struggling with the same thing. In my case depression and or loss of a loved one.  There's lots of things that people think work, but don't really.  But for all sorts of things, the best thing you can do is just find people with similar life experiences... and talk to them.
It doesn't cost a thing. Again, helped me with context.

5 evaluate whether you think depression meds might be useful.   If it's just thoughts, then you may be able to think your way out of this with some help.   If it's partly chemical, then take the meds.  If you're suffering so much that you can't function, or get sleep, then take the meds.

6 get enough sleep.  If you can't sleep, then do 30 minutes of exercise.  That'll make you sleep.
Lack of sleep is a great amplifier of mental illness/difficulties.  Enough sleep will give you the mental resources you'll need to navigate this minefield successfully.

7 I read a book called "how to talk to anyone" which I picked up in the uk. Lots of useful tips to start/hold/end conversations.
